title: Data you can get
objectives: Choose a free data source and note how it differs from the paper’s.

screens.title: The paper's data
screens.prose: This lesson follows Jegadeesh and Titman (1993), "Returns to Buying Winners and Selling Losers" (JT). They use CRSP monthly returns for NYSE and AMEX shares. CRSP keeps every share, including those that later delisted. Here are three places you could look.

state.caption: Where a replicator can get monthly share returns.

screens.question: You want to rebuild JT's sample share by share. Which source can do it?

options.text: CRSP, through WRDS at a university
The French library
options.why: You picked the free source with the right history. It holds ten momentum portfolios already sorted, not the shares inside them.

options.text: yfinance or Stooq
options.why: You picked the easy download. It only knows shares still listed, so every share that died is missing.

hints.text: Which source holds individual shares that no longer trade?
Look at the row for shares that later died.
Only one column says Yes there and also holds share-level returns.

feedback.correct: Correct. Of these three, only CRSP keeps every share and its last return.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the rows for dead shares and for what each source holds.

explain.text: Rebuilding the sample needs each share's returns, dead shares included. The French library is a useful check, but its portfolios are already formed. yfinance and Stooq start from shares alive today.

screens.title: Survivorship
screens.prose: A share that collapsed and delisted in 1975 is not in yfinance. Before it died, its returns were poor for months. We call a sample built only from shares that lived **survivorship-biased**.

state.caption: Where a replicator can get monthly share returns.

screens.question: Which leg of the momentum book loses the most shares, and what does that do to the spread?

options.text: The loser leg; the losers left look better, so the spread is biased down
The loser leg; with fewer losers the spread is biased up
options.why: You counted fewer losers as a gain. The short leg now holds milder losers, which earn more, so selling them earns less.

options.text: The winner leg; dying shares were mostly past winners
options.why: You put dying shares among the winners. A share heading for delisting usually has a poor recent record, so it ranks as a loser.

options.text: Neither; dead shares are rare, so the spread is unchanged
options.why: You assumed the dead are few. Over 25 years many shares delist, and they cluster in the extreme decile we sell.

hints.text: Where does a share rank in the months before it dies?
Poor past returns put it in decile 1, the leg we sell.
Remove the worst losers and the losers' average return rises. Selling a higher return earns less.

feedback.correct: Correct. The short leg loses its worst shares.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask where a share sits in the ranking in its last year.

explain.text: A share near death has poor past returns, so it sits in the loser decile. Dropping it leaves milder losers whose returns are higher. The short leg then earns less, so the spread falls.

screens.title: Delisting returns
screens.prose: CRSP records a delisting return: the share's last return as it leaves the exchange, often a large loss. Some sources keep the prices but drop that final month.

state.caption: Where a replicator can get monthly share returns.

screens.question: Which way does dropping the delisting return move the spread?

options.text: Either way: it raises the return of whichever leg holds the share
Always up, because the losses vanish
options.why: You assumed every lost loss helps the book. A loss that vanishes from the short leg removes a gain we would have made.

options.text: Always down, because dying shares are losers we sell
options.why: You assumed the share is always in the loser leg. Some shares die a few months after ranking as winners.

options.text: Not at all; one month per share is too small to matter
options.why: You treated one month as noise. A delisting return can be −50% or worse, and it lands in an extreme decile.

hints.text: Take a share we hold long, then one we sell short.
A missing −50% helps a long position and hurts a short one.
So the bias raises whichever leg holds the share. Which leg that is varies.

feedback.correct: Correct. The sign depends on which leg held the share.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Follow one dying share in the long leg, then in the short leg.

explain.text: If a winner dies, the long leg misses a loss and looks better. If a loser dies, the short leg misses a gain and the spread looks worse. The net sign is an empirical question, so we state it in the note.

screens.title: Reading the generator
screens.prose: We have no CRSP here, so the course uses a seeded panel: 500 shares, 300 months, seed 2. Month 0 stands for January 1965. You have seen it described. Here are its key lines; `c`, `e` and `d` are 0.015, 0.03 and 0.006.

lines: s = rng.standard_normal((T + L, n)) * sig  # news
cont = sum(s[L-k:L-k+T] for k in range(2, 13))
rev = sum(s[L-k:L-k+T] for k in range(13, 37))
r = 0.004 + beta * m[:, None] + F @ lam.T + idio
params.title: momentum_panel

screens.question: Tap the line that plants momentum: returns that continue in the same direction.

hints.text: Momentum means a shock keeps moving the price for months.
Look for a sum over lags 2 to 12.
Line 4 adds up the shocks from 2 to 12 months back; line 7 multiplies them by c.

feedback.correct: Correct. Each shock adds 1.5% of itself in each of the next 2 to 12 months.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the lags that push returns in the same direction as the shock.

byKey.l5: You tapped the long-horizon sum. Lags 13 to 36 enter with −d: that is reversal, not momentum.
byKey.l6: You tapped the one-month term. −e pulls the next month back: that is reversal.
byKey.l2: You tapped the market. It moves every share together, so ranking cannot profit from it.

explain.text: Line 4 sums the shocks from lags 2 to 12, and line 7 adds c = 1.5% of that sum. Line 6 plants a one-month reversal of −3%. Line 5 with −d plants a slow reversal over months 13 to 36.

screens.title: What the panel plants
screens.prose: Market and factor noise make the spread as noisy as a real one. But we planted the effect ourselves. Share $i$'s return in month $t$, with news shocks $\varepsilon$: $$r_{i,t} = 0.004 + \beta_i m_t + \boldsymbol\lambda_i^{\top}\mathbf f_t + \varepsilon_{i,t} - e\,\varepsilon_{i,t-1} + c\sum_{k=2}^{12}\varepsilon_{i,t-k} - d\sum_{k=13}^{36}\varepsilon_{i,t-k}$$
screens.question: Our replication finds 0.96% a month for 6/6. What does that show?

options.text: That our code recovers an effect we know is there
That momentum exists in share returns
options.why: You read our panel as evidence. We put c = 1.5% in, so finding it says nothing about real markets.

options.text: That the paper's 0.95% is correct
options.why: You treated our panel as an independent check. It was tuned to give a spread of the paper's size.

hints.text: Who chose c = 0.015?
A planted effect is found by correct code by design.
So a match tests the machinery, not the market.

feedback.correct: Correct. Planting is honest for learning the machinery and useless as evidence.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what we knew before we ran the code.

explain.text: We wrote c = 1.5% into the generator, so correct code must find a spread. A match tells us the formation, deciles and cohorts work. Evidence about markets needs real data, which level 3 discusses.

screens.title: Today's index
screens.prose: A colleague replicates momentum from 1990 to 2020. She takes today's S&P 500 members and downloads their full histories. "These are liquid shares, so the data is clean."
screens.question: What is wrong with her universe?

options.text: Every share in it survived to today, so the past losers that died are missing
Nothing; liquid large shares are the right universe
options.why: You judged the data by liquidity. The problem is who is in the list: only shares that lived and grew.

options.text: The period is too short for a 6/6 strategy
options.why: You checked the length. Thirty years is plenty; the selection of shares is the fault.

options.text: Large shares have no momentum at all
options.why: You blamed the size of the shares. Momentum is weaker in large shares, but the fatal flaw is survivorship.

hints.text: When was the list of members chosen?
A 1990 loser that went bust in 1995 cannot be in today's index.
So the universe uses 2020 knowledge to pick 1990 shares.

feedback.correct: Correct. Membership today is information from the future.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask how a share got into today's list.

byKey.liquid: You trusted liquidity. The list itself was chosen with knowledge from 2020: that is survivorship.

explain.text: A share joins today's index by surviving and growing, which is look-ahead. Shares that fell and delisted in between are gone. The loser leg is cleaned, so the spread is biased, as in the dead companies lesson.

screens.title: A missing month
screens.prose: Share B has no return in one month of its formation window, so its formation return is NaN. Here is how the double argsort ranks three shares.

lines: >>> f = np.array([0.05, np.nan, -0.10])  # A, B, C
params.title: Python

screens.question: Where does share B land in the ranking?

options.text: At the top: NaN sorts last, so B ranks as the best winner
At the bottom, as the worst loser
options.why: You read a missing value as a bad one. NumPy sorts NaN to the end, which is the top rank.

options.text: Nowhere: NumPy drops NaN from the sort
options.why: You assumed NumPy skips missing values. argsort keeps them and puts them last.

options.text: In the middle, as an average share
options.why: You imagined NaN treated as typical. NumPy gives it the largest rank.

hints.text: Read the output: which share has rank 2?
Ranks run 0 for the worst to n − 1 for the best.
B gets rank 2 of 0 to 2: the top. So it would be bought as a winner.

feedback.correct: Correct. Unchecked, every NaN formation return ranks as a winner.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read B's rank from the printed array.

explain.text: NumPy sorts NaN after every number, so B gets the top rank. Every share with a missing month would join the winner decile. So we drop a share from a month's ranking unless it has J complete months.

screens.title: Load the panel
screens.prose: In code we treat the seeded panel as our data source. `momentum_panel` is loaded and returns `(r, size, m, F)`. A loader that checks what it loads catches a wrong argument at once.
screens.question: Write `load_panel()` returning `(r, size)` for the base panel, after checking the shape and that no value is NaN.

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np
def momentum_panel(n=500, T=300, seed=2, c=0.015, e=0.03, d=0.006, nf=4, fsd=0.035,
                   c_after=None, t_pub=300, crash=None):
    TMAX, L = 480, 36
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    size = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, n)                 # log size as a z-score
    sig = 0.09 - 0.02 * np.tanh(size)              # small shares are noisier
    beta = rng.uniform(0.5, 1.5, n)
    lam = rng.standard_normal((n, nf))             # loadings on nf style factors
    s = rng.standard_normal((TMAX + L, n))[:T + L] * sig   # news shocks, 36 months burn-in
    m = (0.006 + 0.045 * rng.standard_normal(TMAX))[:T]    # market excess return
    F = (fsd * rng.standard_normal((TMAX, nf)))[:T]        # factor returns
    if crash is not None:                          # a bear market, then a rebound
        m[crash - 12:crash] = -0.03; F[crash - 12:crash, 0] = -0.03
        m[crash:crash + 3] = [0.12, 0.06, 0.04]; F[crash:crash + 3, 0] = [0.12, 0.06, 0.04]
    ct = np.full(T, c)
    if c_after is not None:
        ct[t_pub:] = c_after                       # the effect after publication
    cont = sum(s[L - k:L - k + T] for k in range(2, 13))   # lags 2 to 12: continuation
    rev = sum(s[L - k:L - k + T] for k in range(13, 37))   # lags 13 to 36: reversal
    idio = s[L:L + T] - e * s[L - 1:L - 1 + T] + ct[:, None] * cont - d * rev
    r = 0.004 + beta * m[:, None] + F @ lam.T + idio
    return r, size, m, F                           # r is (T, n) simple monthly returns

widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def drop_short_history(r, J):
    T, n = r.shape
    ok = np.zeros((T, n), dtype=bool)
    for t in range(J, T):
        ok[t] = np.isfinite(r[t - J:t]).all(axis=0)
    return ok

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np
def momentum_panel(n=500, T=300, seed=2, c=0.015, e=0.03, d=0.006, nf=4, fsd=0.035,
                   c_after=None, t_pub=300, crash=None):
    TMAX, L = 480, 36
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    size = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, n)                 # log size as a z-score
    sig = 0.09 - 0.02 * np.tanh(size)              # small shares are noisier
    beta = rng.uniform(0.5, 1.5, n)
    lam = rng.standard_normal((n, nf))             # loadings on nf style factors
    s = rng.standard_normal((TMAX + L, n))[:T + L] * sig   # news shocks, 36 months burn-in
    m = (0.006 + 0.045 * rng.standard_normal(TMAX))[:T]    # market excess return
    F = (fsd * rng.standard_normal((TMAX, nf)))[:T]        # factor returns
    if crash is not None:                          # a bear market, then a rebound
        m[crash - 12:crash] = -0.03; F[crash - 12:crash, 0] = -0.03
        m[crash:crash + 3] = [0.12, 0.06, 0.04]; F[crash:crash + 3, 0] = [0.12, 0.06, 0.04]
    ct = np.full(T, c)
    if c_after is not None:
        ct[t_pub:] = c_after                       # the effect after publication
    cont = sum(s[L - k:L - k + T] for k in range(2, 13))   # lags 2 to 12: continuation
    rev = sum(s[L - k:L - k + T] for k in range(13, 37))   # lags 13 to 36: reversal
    idio = s[L:L + T] - e * s[L - 1:L - 1 + T] + ct[:, None] * cont - d * rev
    r = 0.004 + beta * m[:, None] + F @ lam.T + idio
    return r, size, m, F                           # r is (T, n) simple monthly returns

def formation_returns(r, J, skip=0):
    T = r.shape[0]
    c = np.vstack([np.zeros((1, r.shape[1])), np.cumsum(np.log1p(r), axis=0)])
    f = np.full(r.shape, np.nan)
    for t in range(J + skip, T):
        f[t] = np.expm1(c[t - skip] - c[t - skip - J])
    return f

def cohort_weights(f_t, q=10):
    n = len(f_t)
    rank = np.argsort(np.argsort(f_t, kind="stable"), kind="stable")
    dec = rank * q // n
    top, bot = dec == q - 1, dec == 0
    return np.where(top, 1 / top.sum(), 0.0) - np.where(bot, 1 / bot.sum(), 0.0)

def wml(r, J, K, skip=0):
    T = r.shape[0]
    f = formation_returns(r, J, skip)
    W = np.zeros(r.shape)
    for s in range(J + skip, T):
        W[s] = cohort_weights(f[s])
    out = []
    for t in range(J + skip + K - 1, T):
        out.append(W[t - K + 1:t + 1].mean(axis=0) @ r[t])
    return np.array(out)

quiz.question: Which gap matters most for a momentum replication?

options.text: Shares that delisted are missing
It gives daily, not monthly, prices
options.why: You worried about frequency. Daily prices compound to monthly returns exactly.

options.text: Prices are adjusted for splits
options.why: You flagged the adjustment. Split adjustment is needed for correct returns.

feedback.correct: Correct. Survivorship hits the loser leg.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask which shares the source can never contain.

quiz.prose: On our base panel we flag the bottom 20% of shares by total return as dead and drop them. The one-month spread was 0.52%.
quiz.question: What is it without the dead shares?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Dropping the worst losers lowers what the short leg earns.

byKey.same: You kept the spread unchanged. Removing the dead shares changes who sits in the loser decile.

explain.text: The spread falls from 0.52% to 0.35% a month. The dead shares were mostly losers. Without them the loser leg's return rises, so the spread drops.

quiz.question: What should the code do with D in that month's ranking?

options.text: Leave D out of that month's ranking
Fill the month with a 0% return and rank D
options.why: You invented a return. A 0% guess changes D's rank without any data.

options.text: Rank D anyway; argsort handles NaN
options.why: You trusted argsort. It sorts NaN last, so D would be bought as the top winner.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Recall where argsort puts NaN.

explain.text: argsort puts NaN at the top, so D would join the winners. A filled 0% is a guess dressed as data. Leaving D out for those months is the rule `drop_short_history` encodes.

options.text: We planted the effect, so finding it tests our code, not markets
It has too few shares

options.text: It has no noise
options.why: You assumed a clean panel. Market, factor and idiosyncratic noise make its spread as noisy as a real one.
